title: Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs

paper.title: Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs
paper.abstract: Abstract As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. In this work, we identify three major pitfalls that may lead to misleading conclusions: the lack of heldout evaluation to distinguish genuine concept-wise forgetting from instance-wise overfitting, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training, and unfair method comparisons caused by applying the same training settings to different unlearning methods. To address these challenges, we introduce GEMMU ( G eneralizable E valuation for M ultimodal M achine U nlearning), a benchmark built on real-world knowledge and a principled evaluation protocol. Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods under GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps and challenges conclusions drawn from previous benchmarks. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous evaluation for advancing multimodal machine unlearning and provide guidelines for future benchmark design.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: † † ∗ denotes equal contributions. As MLLMs ( Bai et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, concerns surrounding privacy and data governance have intensified. In this context, machine unlearning has attracted growing attention as a mechanism for removing sensitive or private knowledge, such as personal information, from trained models. As unlearning methods advance, rigorous evaluation is essential to reliably assess their effectiveness. Several benchmarks ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Dontsov et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) have been proposed to assess progress in multimodal machine unlearning. However, we identify the following fundamental pitfalls in existing benchmarks that may lead to overly optimistic or misleading evaluations. First , testing on the training set is widely recognized as poor practice in machine learning, yet existing unlearning protocols often evaluate forgetting and retention on the same data used during unlearning Liu et al. (2025a) ; Ma et al. (2025) ; Zheng et al. (2026) . Such evaluation risks overestimating unlearning effectiveness, as performance on these examples may not generalize to unseen data. This concern is particularly important in the multimodal setting, where effective unlearning should remove knowledge at the concept level rather than merely suppressing specific visual instances . Second , many existing benchmarks ( Dontsov et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Xu et al., 2025 ) focus primarily on newly fine-tuned knowledge, rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training. While convenient for evaluation, such settings may not reflect realistic unlearning scenarios. Moreover, existing unlearning methods largely rely on reverse fine-tuning, which may be more effective at removing newly introduced knowledge. In contrast, pre-trained knowledge is often deeply entangled with other useful knowledge, making it difficult to remove selectively without affecting the model’s general capabilities. As a result, those benchmarks may overestimate the effectiveness of existing methods in real-world unlearning. Figure 1: Three major pitfalls in existing multimodal unlearning benchmarks (top) and how GEMMU addresses them (bottom) through heldout evaluation, real-world knowledge unlearning, and method-specific hyperparameter tuning to achieve generalizable evaluations. Third , most existing benchmarks evaluate different unlearning methods using identical hyperparameters, despite differences in their optimization objectives and training dynamics Xu et al. (2025) ; Dontsov et al. (2025) . A configuration that works well for one method may be suboptimal for another. Consequently, conclusions about which method is more effective can depend on the shared configuration rather than on the methods themselves. To address these limitations, we introduce GEMMU (Generalizable Evaluation for Multimodal Machine Unlearning; Fig. 1 ), a benchmark built on three principles: heldout evaluation for both forget and retain sets, unlearning of real-world pre-trained knowledge, per-method hyperparameter search (Tab. 1 ), and additionally modality gap analysis (Sec. 5.4 ). Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods with GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps overlooked by existing benchmarks, shows that method rankings can change under different configurations, and calls into question the effectiveness of current methods. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify major pitfalls in existing MLLM unlearning evaluations: testing on the training set , reliance on fine-tuned knowledge , and unfair hyperparameter settings across methods. • We introduce GEMMU , a more rigorous benchmark that addresses these limitations and provides principles for future benchmark design. • We re-evaluate nine representative unlearning methods and uncover substantial generalization gaps and ranking changes overlooked by previous benchmarks.

sections.heading: Machine Unlearning Methods for MLLMs
sections.text: Existing approaches to multimodal machine unlearning mainly follow a reverse fine-tuning paradigm, typically suppressing forget-set knowledge through gradient ascent while preserving retained knowledge through gradient descent or other regularization objectives. Representative methods include GA ( Thudi et al., 2022 ) , GADiff ( Liu et al., 2022 ) , KL Min and IDK ( Maini et al., 2024 ) , NPO ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , LLMU ( Yao and Xu, 2024 ) , RMU ( Li et al., 2024b ) , and SCRUB ( Kurmanji et al., 2023 ) . While some of the above methods were originally developed for text-only LLMs, they have served as common baselines for unlearning in MLLMs. More recently, model editing has emerged as an alternative to conventional tuning-based unlearning. For example, MANU ( Liu et al., 2025b ) selectively identifies and prunes model components associated with the knowledge to be forgotten. sections.heading: Machine Unlearning Evaluation for MLLMs
sections.text: Early language-only benchmarks such as TOFU ( Maini et al., 2024 ) establish a controlled evaluation setting for fictitious knowledge removal, and MLLMU-Bench ( Liu et al., 2025a ) extends this direction to multimodal models. CLEAR ( Dontsov et al., 2025 ) , FIUBench ( Ma et al., 2025 ) , UMU-Bench ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , and PEBench ( Xu et al., 2025 ) introduce more comprehensive multimodal evaluation settings covering person profiles, cross-modal knowledge, and personal entities with event scenes. Despite this progress, existing benchmarks remain limited for evaluating practical multimodal unlearning. They still rely on generated identities, which require fine-tuning to memorize this new knowledge and may not reflect the unlearning of real-world, pre-trained knowledge. MMUBench and PEBench ( Li et al., 2024a ; Xu et al., 2025 ) partition the forget set into training and test examples but overlook the same problem for the retain set. An existing preprint, PULSE ( Kawakami et al., 2025 ) , studies the unlearning of pre-trained knowledge, but does not provide a theoretical analysis of the distinction between fine-tuned and pre-trained knowledge, nor does it address overfitting to the forget or retain sets.

sections.heading: Formulation of the Unlearning Task
sections.text: Let f θ f_{\theta} denote an MLLM with parameters θ \theta . Each dataset consists of image-question-answer triplets ( I , q , a ) (I,q,a) , where I I is empty for text-only questions. Given a pre-trained MLLM f θ 0 f_{\theta_{0}} , where θ 0 \theta_{0} denotes the parameters before unlearning, an unlearning method 𝒰 \mathcal{U} updates θ 0 \theta_{0} using the training splits: θ u = 𝒰 ⁡ ( θ 0 , 𝒟 forget train , 𝒟 retain train ) , \theta_{u}=\mathcal{U}(\theta_{0},\mathcal{D}_{\text{forget}}^{\text{train}},\mathcal{D}_{\text{retain}}^{\text{train}}), where θ u \theta_{u} denotes the parameters after unlearning. sections.heading: 4 Pitfalls in Past Evaluations
sections.text: We discuss three major pitfalls in existing multimodal unlearning benchmarks: the lack of proper train-test splits for concept-wise unlearning, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge, and unfair comparisons arising from applying identical hyperparameters across different unlearning methods. All experiments are conducted on our proposed GEMMU dataset, with construction details provided in Sec. 5 .

sections.heading: 4.1 Testing on the Training Set Is Problematic for Concept-wise Unlearning
sections.text: A common practice in prior multimodal unlearning evaluations ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Huo et al., 2025 ; Dontsov et al., 2025 ) is to evaluate forgetting on the same 𝒟 forget \mathcal{D}_{\text{forget}} used during unlearning, and similarly evaluate retention on the same 𝒟 retain \mathcal{D}_{\text{retain}} . Unfortunately, this violates one of the most fundamental principles of machine learning: evaluating generalization on unseen data. A model may appear to forget the target knowledge and retain the rest, while merely overfitting to the examples seen during training. Fig. 2 shows a representative example of overly optimistic training-set evaluation, where accuracy is lower on the forget set and higher on the retain set compared to their respective test sets. One might argue that some prior works additionally evaluate general capabilities on heldout, real-world benchmarks. However, such evaluations do not address the fundamental issue. Without proper train-test splits for both 𝒟 forget \mathcal{D}_{\text{forget}} and 𝒟 retain \mathcal{D}_{\text{retain}} , the reported forgetting and retention scores remain unreliable indicators of unlearning effectiveness, despite being the primary metrics.

sections.heading: Why is this issue more important in multimodal unlearning?
sections.text: In some text-only unlearning scenarios, such as forgetting specific credit card numbers or passwords, the target is an exact string, making training-set evaluation potentially adequate for such instance-wise unlearning . In contrast, the same visual concept (e.g., a photo of Tokyo Tower) can appear in images with different viewpoints, backgrounds, and styles. This introduces greater variation in the input space, making generalization particularly important for concept-wise unlearning . Fig. 3 shows examples where image-text unlearning (concepts provided in images) exhibits a substantially larger generalization gap than text-only unlearning (concepts provided in pure text), highlighting the risk of overestimating forgetting in multimodal machine unlearning when evaluating only on training examples.

sections.heading: 4.2 Reliance on Synthetic, Fine-tuned Knowledge
sections.text: Another key limitation of existing multimodal unlearning benchmarks is their reliance on knowledge introduced through fine-tuning, often in the form of synthetic facts or identities. While such settings offer a controlled environment for evaluating unlearning, they may not accurately reflect the challenges of real-world knowledge removal. In particular, unlearning fine-tuned knowledge and pre-trained knowledge may differ substantially in their underlying dynamics and difficulty. Synthetic knowledge introduced through fine-tuning often consists of relatively isolated facts that are less entangled with the model’s existing knowledge. Reverse fine-tuning , which underlies many existing unlearning algorithms, may provide a relatively straightforward way to undo the effects of fine-tuning and thereby achieve unlearning. In contrast, real-world, pre-trained knowledge is acquired through extensive pre-training and may be deeply entangled with other useful knowledge, making its removal more challenging. As a result, strong performance on synthetic or fine-tuned knowledge does not necessarily translate to effective unlearning of real-world, pre-trained knowledge. To better understand the differences between unlearning pre-trained and fine-tuned knowledge, we investigate both settings from two perspectives: (1) learning dynamics and (2) the forgetting–retention trade-off. These two perspectives provide complementary empirical and theoretical insights into unlearning difficulty. sections.heading: Learning Dynamics.
sections.text: We compare the two settings directly by tracking forget-set performance over unlearning epochs on two matched pairs of GEMMU subsets: real faces versus synthetic identities, and real landmarks versus fictitious ones, where the second subset of each pair is injected into the model through fine-tuning. In Fig. 4 , fine-tuned knowledge drops sharply within the first epoch, whereas pre-trained knowledge decays much more slowly on both LLaVA-1.5-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct. Plots for other unlearning algorithms are provided in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 4.3 Hyperparameter Sensitivity
sections.text: Most existing benchmarks compare unlearning methods under a single shared training configuration (Tab. 1 ). This implicitly assumes that different methods share a common operating range, which we find to be far from true. † † For benchmarks that do not report hyperparameter selection in the paper, we classify them by the hyperparameters in their released code. Fig. 5 compares KL Min and RMU trained under identical shared configurations on LLaVA-1.5-7B, measured by average retain-set minus average forget-set performance on heldout examples, where higher means better forgetting at lower retention cost. At a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} , RMU wins clearly while KL Min appears entirely ineffective; at 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} , the conclusion reverses, with KL Min now outperforming RMU by a wide margin. The same shared protocol thus supports two contradictory conclusions about which algorithm is better. Fig. 6 extends this observation to all nine methods across our search space. Without proper tuning, many configurations lie on the y = x y=x line, i.e., indiscriminate forgetting. After per-method search, the strongest methods fall well below it. This sensitivity partly reflects that multimodal unlearning is harder than text-only unlearning, where a shared configuration is common practice Maini et al. (2024) , and further indicates that fair evaluation for multimodal unlearning requires a per-method hyperparameter search. More examples are provided in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 5 GEMMU
sections.text: GEMMU is designed to reveal the pitfalls discussed in Sec. 4 and to provide practical guidelines that future evaluation benchmarks should follow. Its core components include (1) concept removal of existing real-world knowledge and comparison with fine-tuned knowledge; (2) generalization of forgetting and retention to heldout examples; (3) per-method hyperparameter search for fair comparisons; and additionally, (4) modality gap analysis using image-text and text-only questions, inspired by Wang et al. (2025) and Huo et al. (2025) . We first describe our methodology (Sec. 5.1 ), followed by a re-benchmarking of existing unlearning methods (Sec. 5.4 ), and conclude with design principles for future benchmarks (Sec. 5.5 ).

sections.heading: Concept removal for real-world and synthetic knowledge.
sections.text: To achieve a diverse source of real-world knowledge, we consider human identities, landmarks, car brands, and fruits as our main categories, with 139 concepts in total. Following Liu et al. (2025a) and Wang et al. (2025) , each concept is assigned exclusively to the forget or retain set. We also verified that the evaluated MLLMs have a decent understanding of those concepts before unlearning in Tab. 2 . To compare the unlearning of pre-trained and fine-tuned knowledge in Sec. 4.2 , we additionally include two synthetic knowledge subsets: CLEAR and fake landmarks. For CLEAR, we adopt fictitious identities, along with their associated images and biographical information from the CLEAR dataset ( Dontsov et al., 2025 ) . For fake landmarks, we generate fictional landmark profiles with corresponding images and construct questions about their attributes, including location and completion date. Each synthetic subset consists of 40 concepts. sections.heading: Generalizability analysis.
sections.text: Within each concept, examples are split into disjoint training and test sets, so the test sets assess unseen examples of the same concepts. Images are collected from the Internet and manually verified by the authors. † † We will release the source links instead of the images to prevent copyright infringement. We adopt a train-test split of 5:10, which is less extreme than the single-training-data setup in MMUBench Li et al. (2024a) .

sections.heading: Per-method hyperparameter search.
sections.text: For each method, we search for its optimal hyperparameters by scoring each configuration by its average retain-train minus average forget-train performance and select the configuration with the best score averaged over the four real-world subsets. Selection uses training splits only so that test data never influences it. See Appendix C for the selected hyperparameters and implementation details.

sections.heading: Modality gap analysis.
sections.text: Following Liu et al. (2025a) and Dontsov et al. (2025) , we construct questions in two input modalities: visual question answering (VQA) pairs an image with a textual question, while text-only question answering (QA) contains the concept name and no image. Both modalities cover single-choice classification, fill-in-the-blank, and generation tasks. We use accuracy for classification and fill-in-the-blank tasks and ROUGE-L for generation. For both image-text and text-only tasks, we paraphrase the question texts while preserving their meaning and ground-truth answers to prevent overfitting to the question formats. Representative examples from the forget and retain training and test sets of all six subsets are provided in Appendix E.1 .

sections.heading: 5.2 Participating MLLMs
sections.text: We consider Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct ( Bai et al., 2025 ) and LLaVA-1.5-7B ( Liu et al., 2024 ) as our base MLLMs. Following prior works on multimodal unlearning ( Huo et al., 2025 ; Dontsov et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) , we adopt LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) for both fine-tuning the base models in the synthetic versus pre-trained knowledge experiment and applying the unlearning algorithms.

sections.heading: 5.3 Machine Unlearning Methods
sections.text: We evaluate nine representative machine unlearning methods covering a diverse range of unlearning strategies. Four are built on gradient ascent over forget-set responses: GA ( Thudi et al., 2022 ) uses the ascent loss alone; GADiff ( Liu et al., 2022 ) adds gradient descent on the retain set; KL Min ( Maini et al., 2024 ) instead regularizes retain updates with a KL penalty toward the pre-trained model; and LLMU ( Yao and Xu, 2024 ) further pairs forget prompts with unrelated responses under a KL penalty. NPO ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) replaces unbounded ascent with a preference-style loss whose ascent weight shrinks as the forget loss exceeds the pre-trained loss. IDK ( Maini et al., 2024 ) simply relabels forget answers with abstention targets. SCRUB ( Kurmanji et al., 2023 ) is distillation-based , maximizing KL divergence from a frozen teacher on forget examples while minimizing it on retain examples. Finally, two methods operate on internal representations : RMU ( Li et al., 2024b ) steers forget-set activations at a chosen layer toward a random vector while anchoring retain-set activations, and MANU ( Liu et al., 2025b ) prunes MLP neurons ranked by their forget-versus-retain importance.

sections.heading: 5.4 Re-benchmarking Unlearning Algorithms
sections.text: Table 2 shows results for nine unlearning methods under GEMMU . Our main findings are as follows.

sections.heading: Simple methods win.
sections.text: Recent methods are often reported as state-of-the-art on prior benchmarks. For example, MANU Liu et al. (2025b) outperforms GADiff on MLLMU-Bench Liu et al. (2025a) . Rankings on GEMMU differ: the two strongest methods are among the oldest and simplest, GADiff and SCRUB.

sections.heading: Association removal vs. concept removal.
sections.text: The two modalities reveal what is unlearned. Following the notion in Huo et al. (2025) , if only VQA drops while QA survives, the model has merely severed the association between visual appearance and knowledge; if both drop, the concept itself is removed. Tab. 3 classifies each method by comparing its VQA and QA drops on the forget-test split based on the results in Tab. 2 . RMU is the clearest association remover: on Qwen3-VL-8B, VQA classification falls to 2.48 while QA stays at 83.91 (FITB: 1.66 vs. 76.88), so the model no longer recognizes the visual entity but still knows everything about it. GADiff removes whole concepts, at the cost of the largest retain-side drop.

sections.heading: No method solves the task.
sections.text: Even the best entries in Table 2 fall short of ideal unlearning: GADiff sacrifices retain classification (48.49 on LLaVA, 56.7 on Qwen), SCRUB leaves textual forget knowledge largely intact, and the remaining methods either under-forgets or over-destroys. We conclude that unlearning real-world, pre-trained multimodal knowledge remains unsolved.

sections.heading: 5.5 On Guidelines for Future Multimodal Unlearning Benchmarks
sections.text: We close by distilling our findings into design guidance, in the hope that good practices are inherited by future benchmarks.

sections.heading: What makes a good design?
sections.text: First, the fundamentals of machine learning evaluation: a proper train–test split, so that forgetting and retention are measured as generalization rather than memorization (Sec. 4.1 ), and a hyperparameter search per method, without which conclusions about relative effectiveness may reflect the chosen configuration rather than the methods themselves (Sec. 4.3 ). Second, echoing modality-gap studies in multimodal unlearning ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Huo et al., 2025 ) , benchmarks should construct and report both VQA and QA metrics for every task. Only the contrast between the two reveals whether a method removes the visual–textual association or the concept itself (Sec. 5.4 ).

sections.heading: What to avoid?
sections.text: Inheriting text-only practices without accounting for what is unique to MLLMs: instance-wise forgetting may be defensible for text, but not for concept-wise forgetting in MLLMs (Fig. 3 ). Likewise, convenience should not trump rigor. Benchmarks built on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge are easier to construct but may not reflect realistic unlearning (Sec. 4.2 ), and applying one shared hyperparameter configuration to every method can distort the comparison (Sec. 4.3 ).

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we introduce GEMMU , a benchmark for multimodal machine unlearning that emphasizes generalization-aware evaluation and covers a broader and more diverse range of real-world concepts than prior benchmarks. Experiments on GEMMU reveal substantial generalization gaps overlooked by previous benchmarks, highlight the challenges of removing pre-trained knowledge that is deeply entangled with retained knowledge, and demonstrate how proper hyperparameter tuning can alter the relative rankings of unlearning methods. As unlearning methods and benchmarks become increasingly sophisticated, we emphasize that fundamental principles of evaluation must not be overlooked to ensure that scientific progress is built on a solid foundation.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Following common practice in existing multimodal unlearning work, we use LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) for both fine-tuning and unlearning. Full-model fine-tuning may exhibit different unlearning behavior from adapter-based fine-tuning. However, we do not extend our experiments to full-model fine-tuning due to its substantially higher computational cost, and instead focus on settings that can be feasibly evaluated on an NVIDIA H100 GPU.

sections.heading: Practical Interpretation of the Assumptions.
sections.text: Assumptions A1–A3 provide sufficient conditions for a local forgetting–retention trade-off. A1 bounds the sensitivity of the target knowledge score, A2 constrains the gradient of retained utility, and A3 imposes a quadratic retention penalty under parameter changes. We acknowledge that A3 is a strong assumption, and therefore the derived bound should be interpreted as a conditional theoretical result rather than a universal guarantee of retention degradation.

sections.heading: C.1 Hyperparameter and checkpoint selection
sections.text: We base our default hyperparameters on MMUnlearner ( Huo et al., 2025 ) and tune each method using only training results. We favor settings that keep retain-set performance high and forget-set performance low, using Selection score \displaystyle\text{Selection score} = mean retain-train score \displaystyle=\text{mean retain-train score} − mean forget-train score . \displaystyle-\text{mean forget-train score}. Higher is better. For each subset, the means give equal weight to classification accuracy, fill-in-the-blank accuracy, and ROUGE-L, and to image-text and text-only inputs. Accuracies are expressed as percentages and ROUGE-L is multiplied by 100, putting all three metrics on a 0–100 scale. Hyperparameters are selected on training splits only to prevent the obvious test-set leakage. Due to the low number (five) of training images per concept, we do not further split the training set into training and validations sets. † † For benchmarks that have a larger number of training images, it would be beneficial to create such a validation set. For each candidate configuration, we score every checkpoint (epoch) by the difference between its average retain-train performance and its average forget-train performance, where both averages span the six task–modality metrics (three tasks × \times VQA/QA). For each of the four real-world subsets (human identities, car brands, fruits, and landmarks), we take the best score across epochs, and the configuration with the highest average of these four scores is selected. Under the selected configuration, the reported checkpoint is then chosen per subset as the epoch with the highest score. The synthetic subsets (CLEAR and fake landmarks) reuse the selected configuration and choose their own epochs, but do not influence the configuration choice. For both LLaVA-1.5-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct experiments, we use a batch size of 2, random seed 42, and 8 training epochs. LoRA uses rank 16, scaling parameter 16, and dropout 0.05.

Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs Oscar Chew Po-Yi Lu Yi-Jie Cheng Kunal Jain Affiliation: Texas A&M University National Taiwan University Columbia University Hsuan-Tien Lin Zhengzhong Tu Kuan-Hao Huang Email: {oscarchew,kjain,tzz,khhuang}@tamu.edu{d09944015,htlin}@csie.ntu.edu.tw yc4708@columbia.edu Abstract As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. In this work, we identify three major pitfalls that may lead to misleading conclusions: the lack of heldout evaluation to distinguish genuine concept-wise forgetting from instance-wise overfitting, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training, and unfair method comparisons caused by applying the same training settings to different unlearning methods. To address these challenges, we introduce GEMMU ( G eneralizable E valuation for M ultimodal M achine U nlearning), a benchmark built on real-world knowledge and a principled evaluation protocol. Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods under GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps and challenges conclusions drawn from previous benchmarks. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous evaluation for advancing multimodal machine unlearning and provide guidelines for future benchmark design. 1 Introduction † † ∗ denotes equal contributions. As MLLMs ( Bai et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, concerns surrounding privacy and data governance have intensified. In this context, machine unlearning has attracted growing attention as a mechanism for removing sensitive or private knowledge, such as personal information, from trained models. As unlearning methods advance, rigorous evaluation is essential to reliably assess their effectiveness. Several benchmarks ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Dontsov et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) have been proposed to assess progress in multimodal machine unlearning. However, we identify the following fundamental pitfalls in existing benchmarks that may lead to overly optimistic or misleading evaluations. First , testing on the training set is widely recognized as poor practice in machine learning, yet existing unlearning protocols often evaluate forgetting and retention on the same data used during unlearning Liu et al. (2025a) ; Ma et al. (2025) ; Zheng et al. (2026) . Such evaluation risks overestimating unlearning effectiveness, as performance on these examples may not generalize to unseen data. This concern is particularly important in the multimodal setting, where effective unlearning should remove knowledge at the concept level rather than merely suppressing specific visual instances . Second , many existing benchmarks ( Dontsov et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Xu et al., 2025 ) focus primarily on newly fine-tuned knowledge, rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training. While convenient for evaluation, such settings may not reflect realistic unlearning scenarios. Moreover, existing unlearning methods largely rely on reverse fine-tuning, which may be more effective at removing newly introduced knowledge. In contrast, pre-trained knowledge is often deeply entangled with other useful knowledge, making it difficult to remove selectively without affecting the model’s general capabilities. As a result, those benchmarks may overestimate the effectiveness of existing methods in real-world unlearning. Figure 1: Three major pitfalls in existing multimodal unlearning benchmarks (top) and how GEMMU addresses them (bottom) through heldout evaluation, real-world knowledge unlearning, and method-specific hyperparameter tuning to achieve generalizable evaluations. Third , most existing benchmarks evaluate different unlearning methods using identical hyperparameters, despite differences in their optimization objectives and training dynamics Xu et al. (2025) ; Dontsov et al. (2025) . A configuration that works well for one method may be suboptimal for another. Consequently, conclusions about which method is more effective can depend on the shared configuration rather than on the methods themselves. To address these limitations, we introduce GEMMU (Generalizable Evaluation for Multimodal Machine Unlearning; Fig. 1 ), a benchmark built on three principles: heldout evaluation for both forget and retain sets, unlearning of real-world pre-trained knowledge, per-method hyperparameter search (Tab. 1 ), and additionally modality gap analysis (Sec. 5.4 ). Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods with GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps overlooked by existing benchmarks, shows that method rankings can change under different configurations, and calls into question the effectiveness of current methods. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify major pitfalls in existing MLLM unlearning evaluations: testing on the training set , reliance on fine-tuned knowledge , and unfair hyperparameter settings across methods. • We introduce GEMMU , a more rigorous benchmark that addresses these limitations and provides principles for future benchmark design. • We re-evaluate nine representative unlearning methods and uncover substantial generalization gaps and ranking changes overlooked by previous benchmarks. 2 Related Works Machine Unlearning Methods for MLLMs Existing approaches to multimodal machine unlearning mainly follow a reverse fine-tuning paradigm, typically suppressing forget-set knowledge through gradient ascent while preserving retained knowledge through gradient descent or other regularization objectives. Representative methods include GA ( Thudi et al., 2022 ) , GADiff ( Liu et al., 2022 ) , KL Min and IDK ( Maini et al., 2024 ) , NPO ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , LLMU ( Yao and Xu, 2024 ) , RMU ( Li et al., 2024b ) , and SCRUB ( Kurmanji et al., 2023 ) . While some of the above methods were originally developed for text-only LLMs, they have served as common baselines for unlearning in MLLMs. More recently, model editing has emerged as an alternative to conventional tuning-based unlearning. For example, MANU ( Liu et al., 2025b ) selectively identifies and prunes model components associated with the knowledge to be forgotten. Machine Unlearning Evaluation for MLLMs Early language-only benchmarks such as TOFU ( Maini et al., 2024 ) establish a controlled evaluation setting for fictitious knowledge removal, and MLLMU-Bench ( Liu et al., 2025a ) extends this direction to multimodal models. CLEAR ( Dontsov et al., 2025 ) , FIUBench ( Ma et al., 2025 ) , UMU-Bench ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , and PEBench ( Xu et al., 2025 ) introduce more comprehensive multimodal evaluation settings covering person profiles, cross-modal knowledge, and personal entities with event scenes. Despite this progress, existing benchmarks remain limited for evaluating practical multimodal unlearning. They still rely on generated identities, which require fine-tuning to memorize this new knowledge and may not reflect the unlearning of real-world, pre-trained knowledge. MMUBench and PEBench ( Li et al., 2024a ; Xu et al., 2025 ) partition the forget set into training and test examples but overlook the same problem for the retain set. An existing preprint, PULSE ( Kawakami et al., 2025 ) , studies the unlearning of pre-trained knowledge, but does not provide a theoretical analysis of the distinction between fine-tuned and pre-trained knowledge, nor does it address overfitting to the forget or retain sets. 3 Preliminaries Formulation of the Unlearning Task Let f θ f_{\theta} denote an MLLM with parameters θ \theta . Following the standard formulation in this field, the unlearning task considers two datasets: a forget set 𝒟 forget \mathcal{D}_{\text{forget}} , containing knowledge to be removed, and a retain set 𝒟 retain \mathcal{D}_{\text{retain}} , containing knowledge to be preserved. Each dataset consists of image-question-answer triplets ( I , q , a ) (I,q,a) , where I I is empty for text-only questions. We further partition both datasets into disjoint training and test sets to evaluate generalizability: 𝒟 forget train , 𝒟 forget test , 𝒟 retain train \mathcal{D}_{\text{forget}}^{\text{train}},\mathcal{D}_{\text{forget}}^{\text{test}},\mathcal{D}_{\text{retain}}^{\text{train}} and 𝒟 retain test \mathcal{D}_{\text{retain}}^{\text{test}} . Given a pre-trained MLLM f θ 0 f_{\theta_{0}} , where θ 0 \theta_{0} denotes the parameters before unlearning, an unlearning method 𝒰 \mathcal{U} updates θ 0 \theta_{0} using the training splits: θ u = 𝒰 ⁡ ( θ 0 , 𝒟 forget train , 𝒟 retain train ) , \theta_{u}=\mathcal{U}(\theta_{0},\mathcal{D}_{\text{forget}}^{\text{train}},\mathcal{D}_{\text{retain}}^{\text{train}}), where θ u \theta_{u} denotes the parameters after unlearning. Note that previous works often use the entire 𝒟 forget \mathcal{D}_{\text{forget}} and 𝒟 retain \mathcal{D}_{\text{retain}} in place of the training splits mentioned above. The objective is to reduce the model’s ability to recover knowledge in 𝒟 forget \mathcal{D}_{\text{forget}} , while preserving its performance on 𝒟 retain \mathcal{D}_{\text{retain}} . Successful unlearning should achieve these goals not only on the training splits but also on the test splits, which provide a more reliable measure of generalizable forgetting and knowledge retention. Image-text unlearning exhibits a substantially larger generalization gap than text-only unlearning, despite using the same dataset and training configurations. 4 Pitfalls in Past Evaluations We discuss three major pitfalls in existing multimodal unlearning benchmarks: the lack of proper train-test splits for concept-wise unlearning, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge, and unfair comparisons arising from applying identical hyperparameters across different unlearning methods. All experiments are conducted on our proposed GEMMU dataset, with construction details provided in Sec. 5 . 4.1 Testing on the Training Set Is Problematic for Concept-wise Unlearning A common practice in prior multimodal unlearning evaluations ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Huo et al., 2025 ; Dontsov et al., 2025 ) is to evaluate forgetting on the same 𝒟 forget \mathcal{D}_{\text{forget}} used during unlearning, and similarly evaluate retention on the same 𝒟 retain \mathcal{D}_{\text{retain}} . Unfortunately, this violates one of the most fundamental principles of machine learning: evaluating generalization on unseen data. A model may appear to forget the target knowledge and retain the rest, while merely overfitting to the examples seen during training. Fig. 2 shows a representative example of overly optimistic training-set evaluation, where accuracy is lower on the forget set and higher on the retain set compared to their respective test sets. One might argue that some prior works additionally evaluate general capabilities on heldout, real-world benchmarks. However, such evaluations do not address the fundamental issue. Without proper train-test splits for both 𝒟 forget \mathcal{D}_{\text{forget}} and 𝒟 retain \mathcal{D}_{\text{retain}} , the reported forgetting and retention scores remain unreliable indicators of unlearning effectiveness, despite being the primary metrics. Why is this issue more important in multimodal unlearning? In some text-only unlearning scenarios, such as forgetting specific credit card numbers or passwords, the target is an exact string, making training-set evaluation potentially adequate for such instance-wise unlearning . In contrast, the same visual concept (e.g., a photo of Tokyo Tower) can appear in images with different viewpoints, backgrounds, and styles. This introduces greater variation in the input space, making generalization particularly important for concept-wise unlearning . Fig. 3 shows examples where image-text unlearning (concepts provided in images) exhibits a substantially larger generalization gap than text-only unlearning (concepts provided in pure text), highlighting the risk of overestimating forgetting in multimodal machine unlearning when evaluating only on training examples. 4.2 Reliance on Synthetic, Fine-tuned Knowledge Another key limitation of existing multimodal unlearning benchmarks is their reliance on knowledge introduced through fine-tuning, often in the form of synthetic facts or identities. While such settings offer a controlled environment for evaluating unlearning, they may not accurately reflect the challenges of real-world knowledge removal. In particular, unlearning fine-tuned knowledge and pre-trained knowledge may differ substantially in their underlying dynamics and difficulty. Synthetic knowledge introduced through fine-tuning often consists of relatively isolated facts that are less entangled with the model’s existing knowledge. Reverse fine-tuning , which underlies many existing unlearning algorithms, may provide a relatively straightforward way to undo the effects of fine-tuning and thereby achieve unlearning. In contrast, real-world, pre-trained knowledge is acquired through extensive pre-training and may be deeply entangled with other useful knowledge, making its removal more challenging. As a result, strong performance on synthetic or fine-tuned knowledge does not necessarily translate to effective unlearning of real-world, pre-trained knowledge. To better understand the differences between unlearning pre-trained and fine-tuned knowledge, we investigate both settings from two perspectives: (1) learning dynamics and (2) the forgetting–retention trade-off. These two perspectives provide complementary empirical and theoretical insights into unlearning difficulty. This implicitly assumes that different methods share a common operating range, which we find to be far from true. † † For benchmarks that do not report hyperparameter selection in the paper, we classify them by the hyperparameters in their released code. Fig. 5 compares KL Min and RMU trained under identical shared configurations on LLaVA-1.5-7B, measured by average retain-set minus average forget-set performance on heldout examples, where higher means better forgetting at lower retention cost. At a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} , RMU wins clearly while KL Min appears entirely ineffective; at 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} , the conclusion reverses, with KL Min now outperforming RMU by a wide margin. The same shared protocol thus supports two contradictory conclusions about which algorithm is better. Fig. 6 extends this observation to all nine methods across our search space. Without proper tuning, many configurations lie on the y = x y=x line, i.e., indiscriminate forgetting. After per-method search, the strongest methods fall well below it. This sensitivity partly reflects that multimodal unlearning is harder than text-only unlearning, where a shared configuration is common practice Maini et al. (2024) , and further indicates that fair evaluation for multimodal unlearning requires a per-method hyperparameter search. More examples are provided in Appendix D . 5 GEMMU GEMMU is designed to reveal the pitfalls discussed in Sec. 4 and to provide practical guidelines that future evaluation benchmarks should follow. Its core components include (1) concept removal of existing real-world knowledge and comparison with fine-tuned knowledge; (2) generalization of forgetting and retention to heldout examples; (3) per-method hyperparameter search for fair comparisons; and additionally, (4) modality gap analysis using image-text and text-only questions, inspired by Wang et al. (2025) and Huo et al. (2025) . We first describe our methodology (Sec. 5.1 ), followed by a re-benchmarking of existing unlearning methods (Sec. 5.4 ), and conclude with design principles for future benchmarks (Sec. 5.5 ). 5.1 Benchmark Construction Concept removal for real-world and synthetic knowledge. To achieve a diverse source of real-world knowledge, we consider human identities, landmarks, car brands, and fruits as our main categories, with 139 concepts in total. Following Liu et al. (2025a) and Wang et al. (2025) , each concept is assigned exclusively to the forget or retain set. We also verified that the evaluated MLLMs have a decent understanding of those concepts before unlearning in Tab. 2 . To compare the unlearning of pre-trained and fine-tuned knowledge in Sec. 4.2 , we additionally include two synthetic knowledge subsets: CLEAR and fake landmarks. For CLEAR, we adopt fictitious identities, along with their associated images and biographical information from the CLEAR dataset ( Dontsov et al., 2025 ) . Four are built on gradient ascent over forget-set responses: GA ( Thudi et al., 2022 ) uses the ascent loss alone; GADiff ( Liu et al., 2022 ) adds gradient descent on the retain set; KL Min ( Maini et al., 2024 ) instead regularizes retain updates with a KL penalty toward the pre-trained model; and LLMU ( Yao and Xu, 2024 ) further pairs forget prompts with unrelated responses under a KL penalty. NPO ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) replaces unbounded ascent with a preference-style loss whose ascent weight shrinks as the forget loss exceeds the pre-trained loss. IDK ( Maini et al., 2024 ) simply relabels forget answers with abstention targets. SCRUB ( Kurmanji et al., 2023 ) is distillation-based , maximizing KL divergence from a frozen teacher on forget examples while minimizing it on retain examples. Finally, two methods operate on internal representations : RMU ( Li et al., 2024b ) steers forget-set activations at a chosen layer toward a random vector while anchoring retain-set activations, and MANU ( Liu et al., 2025b ) prunes MLP neurons ranked by their forget-versus-retain importance. 5.4 Re-benchmarking Unlearning Algorithms Table 2 shows results for nine unlearning methods under GEMMU . RMU is the clearest association remover: on Qwen3-VL-8B, VQA classification falls to 2.48 while QA stays at 83.91 (FITB: 1.66 vs. 76.88), so the model no longer recognizes the visual entity but still knows everything about it. GADiff removes whole concepts, at the cost of the largest retain-side drop. No method solves the task. Even the best entries in Table 2 fall short of ideal unlearning: GADiff sacrifices retain classification (48.49 on LLaVA, 56.7 on Qwen), SCRUB leaves textual forget knowledge largely intact, and the remaining methods either under-forgets or over-destroys. We conclude that unlearning real-world, pre-trained multimodal knowledge remains unsolved. 5.5 On Guidelines for Future Multimodal Unlearning Benchmarks We close by distilling our findings into design guidance, in the hope that good practices are inherited by future benchmarks. What makes a good design? First, the fundamentals of machine learning evaluation: a proper train–test split, so that forgetting and retention are measured as generalization rather than memorization (Sec. 4.1 ), and a hyperparameter search per method, without which conclusions about relative effectiveness may reflect the chosen configuration rather than the methods themselves (Sec. 4.3 ). Second, echoing modality-gap studies in multimodal unlearning ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Huo et al., 2025 ) , benchmarks should construct and report both VQA and QA metrics for every task. Only the contrast between the two reveals whether a method removes the visual–textual association or the concept itself (Sec. 5.4 ). What to avoid? Inheriting text-only practices without accounting for what is unique to MLLMs: instance-wise forgetting may be defensible for text, but not for concept-wise forgetting in MLLMs (Fig. 3 ). Likewise, convenience should not trump rigor. Benchmarks built on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge are easier to construct but may not reflect realistic unlearning (Sec. 4.2 ), and applying one shared hyperparameter configuration to every method can distort the comparison (Sec. 4.3 ). 6 Conclusion In this work, we introduce GEMMU , a benchmark for multimodal machine unlearning that emphasizes generalization-aware evaluation and covers a broader and more diverse range of real-world concepts than prior benchmarks. Experiments on GEMMU reveal substantial generalization gaps overlooked by previous benchmarks, highlight the challenges of removing pre-trained knowledge that is deeply entangled with retained knowledge, and demonstrate how proper hyperparameter tuning can alter the relative rankings of unlearning methods. As unlearning methods and benchmarks become increasingly sophisticated, we emphasize that fundamental principles of evaluation must not be overlooked to ensure that scientific progress is built on a solid foundation. Limitations Following common practice in existing multimodal unlearning work, we use LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) for both fine-tuning and unlearning. Full-model fine-tuning may exhibit different unlearning behavior from adapter-based fine-tuning. However, we do not extend our experiments to full-model fine-tuning due to its substantially higher computational cost, and instead focus on settings that can be feasibly evaluated on an NVIDIA H100 GPU. Higher is better. For each subset, the means give equal weight to classification accuracy, fill-in-the-blank accuracy, and ROUGE-L, and to image-text and text-only inputs. Accuracies are expressed as percentages and ROUGE-L is multiplied by 100, putting all three metrics on a 0–100 scale. Hyperparameters are selected on training splits only to prevent the obvious test-set leakage. Due to the low number (five) of training images per concept, we do not further split the training set into training and validations sets. † † For benchmarks that have a larger number of training images, it would be beneficial to create such a validation set. For each candidate configuration, we score every checkpoint (epoch) by the difference between its average retain-train performance and its average forget-train performance, where both averages span the six task–modality metrics (three tasks × \times VQA/QA). The synthetic subsets (CLEAR and fake landmarks) reuse the selected configuration and choose their own epochs, but do not influence the configuration choice.
